title: A sorted map for the whole web
teaches: Log-structured storage (memtable, SSTables, compaction, Bloom filters), splitting by key range, and choosing a row key
summary: **Bigtable is a sorted map.** A value is found by row key, column and timestamp, rows are kept in key order, and only a single row can be changed atomically.
**Write the queries down before the schema.** The row key decides which rows sit together, so it should be chosen from the reads the table must answer.

**A log-structured store turns random writes into sequential ones.** Each write is appended to a commit log and put in a sorted table in memory, and a full memtable is written out whole as an immutable SSTable.
**A read merges the memtable with every SSTable.** Without help, a lookup costs one disk read per file, so files must be merged and skipped.
**Compaction merges SSTables in the background.** It keeps reads cheap and drops deleted data, at the price of writing the same bytes to disk several times.
**A Bloom filter answers "definitely not here" from memory.** About 10 bits per key give a 1% false-positive rate, so a lookup reads only the file that holds the row.
**Tables are split by row range into tablets of 100 to 200 MB.** Each tablet is served by one tablet server, so related rows can be scanned together.
**A row key that starts with the time sends every new write to one tablet.** A prefix such as an entity ID or a hash spreads the writes, at the cost of scans by time.
**Range partitioning and hash partitioning trade scans for balance.** Ranges keep neighbours together but make hot spots; hashes spread load but scatter every range query.

blocks.text: In November 2006, at the OSDI conference in Seattle, nine Google engineers, with Fay Chang as first author and Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat among them, presented "Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data". By then Bigtable held the data of more than sixty Google products and projects. The web index kept every crawled page in it, Google Earth kept its satellite imagery, Google Analytics kept the clicks it counted for websites, and Personalized Search kept each user's history.

Those products had very different access patterns. Earth's tiles were large and read in bulk; Analytics wrote billions of tiny records and read them back as summaries; the web crawler rewrote each page whenever it was fetched again and retained the older versions for a set period. They all stored petabytes of data and needed to run small reads and writes at high throughput. GFS (lessons 6 and 7) stores large files that clients mostly append to and read in long streams. It can overwrite bytes at an offset, but slowly and with no index to locate individual records, making it unsuitable for updating small records one at a time.

One hardware constraint drove most of the design. A spinning disk in 2006 took about 10 ms to seek to a new position, limiting it to about 100 random writes per second. The same disk could write sequentially at 50 to 100 MB/s, which is 50,000 to 100,000 records of 1 KB per second. Updating records in place requires a disk seek on every write, whereas appending new data runs at the disk's sequential bandwidth, which is 500 to 1,000 times higher. GFS already supported fast appends. The engineers needed to build a storage engine that handled random updates using only sequential appends and immutable files.

When you design a Bigtable schema, you start with the read queries. Consider the web crawler, which was one of Bigtable's first applications. It must answer three main queries: fetch the latest copy of a single page, fetch every page belonging to a single site (such as cnn.com), and find the anchor text of every incoming link to a page, which the search indexer uses to infer what the page is about. A table optimised for those three reads has a different layout from a table built for another workload, and in Bigtable the **row key** determines most of that layout.

The authors describe a Bigtable as a sparse, distributed, persistent, multidimensional sorted map. You look up a value by three coordinates (a row key, a column and a timestamp), and the value is an uninterpreted array of bytes. Bigtable keeps rows sorted lexicographically by key, so all rows whose keys share a prefix sit contiguously on disk and can be read in a single scan. You group columns into a small number of **families** declared up front, such as `contents` or `anchor`. Within a family, a client can create any number of columns on the fly simply by writing to a `family:qualifier` name. If a row has no value in a given column, Bigtable stores nothing for it, which is why the map is called sparse.

blocks.caption: One row of the paper's example, the Webtable. The row key is the page's URL with the host name reversed, so all of CNN's pages sort together. The contents column keeps three versions of the page; the anchor family has one column for each page linking here, holding the link's text.

blocks.text: This layout serves the crawler's three read queries directly. The latest copy of a page is the newest version in its `contents` column. Fetching every page of a site takes a single scan because the row key begins with the reversed hostname (`com.cnn.www`), making `com.cnn.` a shared prefix for every page under `cnn.com`. If you stored the URL as written, `www.cnn.com` would sort among millions of other `www` keys and its pages would sit far apart from `money.cnn.com`. Incoming links to a page are stored in that page's own row inside the `anchor` family, so reading all of them takes a single row lookup rather than a scan of the entire web. By listing the three read queries first, you can choose the row key and column families to match them.

The client API is small. A client can write or delete cells in a row, read a single row, and scan a contiguous range of rows while filtering by column. Each cell stores multiple versions indexed by **timestamp**, a 64-bit integer representing microseconds (assigned either by Bigtable or by the client), and each column family configures its own garbage-collection rule, such as keeping only the latest three versions or versions newer than seven days. Any read or write within a single row is atomic, regardless of how many columns it modifies. Bigtable does not support transactions across multiple rows, a trade-off we will revisit in later lessons.[^rows]

Inside Bigtable, a server stores the data for a range of rows in a **log-structured merge tree** (LSM tree), a data structure introduced by Patrick O'Neil and his colleagues in 1996. It has one component in memory and two on disk.

When a write arrives, the server first appends it to a [[commit log|write]] stored in GFS, making the write durable. Next, the server inserts the data into the **memtable**, an in-memory sorted map where insertions take only a few microseconds. When the memtable reaches a configured size threshold, the server freezes it, creates a fresh memtable for new writes, and flushes the frozen memtable to GFS in key order as a single **SSTable** (Sorted String Table) file. Serving this write requires no random disk seeks to a fixed location for the row, because no fixed location exists. Instead, the versions of a row are spread across the memtable and whichever SSTables happen to contain updates for that key.

blocks.caption: An SSTable on disk: sorted key and value pairs in blocks of about 64 KB, a block index giving each block's last key, and an optional Bloom filter. An SSTable is never modified; it is only read, and eventually replaced.

blocks.text: SSTables are **immutable**: once written to GFS, they are never modified in place. Updating a row simply inserts a newer timestamped entry into the memtable, which later flushes to a newer SSTable. Deleting a key writes a special marker called a **tombstone**, which shadows older versions of the data until a background pass removes them.[^tombstone] Because SSTables never change, servers can cache, copy, compress[^bmdiff] and share them without locks, and the access pattern matches GFS, which is optimised for writing whole files sequentially rather than overwriting blocks in place.

This write performance comes at the expense of reads. To read a row, a Bigtable server must check the memtable and every SSTable that might contain a version of that key, scanning from newest to oldest and merging the results. Checking a single SSTable is fast if its block index is cached in memory: the server runs a binary search on the index to identify a single 64 KB block and issues one disk read to fetch it. Even so, checking many files adds up. The 2006 paper's single-server benchmark shows the asymmetry: one tablet server handled 8,831 random 1 KB writes per second, but only 1,212 random 1 KB reads per second, because the reads waited on disk seeks across GFS while the writes went straight to the commit log and memory.

Without maintenance, SSTables accumulate indefinitely as memtables flush, forcing every read to check more and more files. **Compaction** bounds the number of files. In the background, a tablet server reads several SSTables, merges their sorted streams in key order, retains only the versions allowed by each column family's retention policy, and writes out a single new SSTable to replace the inputs. Because the inputs and output are sorted, the merge reads and writes sequentially at full disk bandwidth. A compaction that merges all SSTables for a row range into a single file also discards tombstones and the deleted versions beneath them; the Bigtable authors call this a major compaction.

blocks.caption: One tablet's writes, as a time lapse. The memtable fills at the write rate and is flushed as a 64 MB SSTable; with compaction on, four tables of one size are merged into one. The bars at the bottom count disk reads for a lookup that misses the memtable. In this simplified model, sizes and rules are fixed; real production stores vary them.
blocks.task: Turn compaction off and play until the files pile up, then turn Bloom filters on.

blocks.text: The simulation illustrates the three overhead metrics that every log-structured storage engine must balance. **Read amplification** is the number of files a point lookup or scan must check; without compaction, it grows with every memtable flush. **Write amplification** is the ratio of bytes written to underlying storage to bytes written by the client: each record is written once to the commit log, once when flushed to an SSTable, and again during every compaction that includes it. **Space amplification** is the extra disk space occupied by stale versions and deleted records waiting to be compacted away. Compacting aggressively reduces read and space amplification at the cost of higher write amplification; compacting lazily does the opposite. Later storage engines provide multiple compaction strategies to tune this trade-off. Write-heavy workloads typically use a memtable of tens of megabytes (64 MB in the figure) with **size-tiered** compaction, which merges SSTables of similar size. Read-heavy workloads often use **leveled** compaction, which organises files into non-overlapping key ranges at each level so reads check fewer files, at the cost of rewriting bytes more frequently. Under either strategy, a background compaction saturating disk bandwidth can cause the tail-latency spikes discussed in lesson 9.

A second optimisation allows a server to skip SSTables that do not contain the requested key without reading them from disk. A **Bloom filter**, invented by Burton Bloom in 1970, is an in-memory bit array paired with $k$ independent hash functions. When writing an SSTable, the server hashes each key $k$ ways and sets the corresponding $k$ bits in the array to 1. Before reading an SSTable from disk, the server hashes the lookup key the same $k$ ways: if any of those $k$ bits is 0, the key is definitely not in the file; if all $k$ bits are 1, the key is probably present. Allocating 10 bits per key yields a false-positive rate just under 1%, meaning a filter for one million keys takes only 1.2 MB of memory.[^bloom] When you attach a Bloom filter to every SSTable, a point lookup checks the filters in memory first and reads from disk only when a filter returns true. Lookups for keys that exist in a single SSTable require about one disk read, and lookups for non-existent keys rarely touch the disk at all.

Engineers outside Google soon adopted the same architecture. Dean and Ghemawat implemented the single-machine storage engine as an open-source library called LevelDB in 2011; Facebook forked LevelDB in 2012 to create RocksDB, adding leveled compaction and concurrency optimisations; Apache HBase replicated Bigtable's distributed design on top of the Hadoop Distributed File System; and Apache Cassandra (lesson 12) uses an LSM engine on each node. Whenever documentation describes a database as "LSM-based", it uses this architecture.

Bigtable partitions each table horizontally by row key into contiguous ranges called **tablets**, typically sized between 100 MB and 200 MB. Because the table is sorted, a tablet is defined simply by its start key and end key. Each tablet is assigned to a single **tablet server**, which holds the tablet's memtable in RAM and reads and writes its SSTables in GFS; a single tablet server typically manages between ten and a thousand tablets. When a tablet grows past the size limit, the tablet server splits it at a median key into two tablets, which the master can then assign to different servers.

A single master process assigns tablets to tablet servers and migrates them to balance load, just as the GFS master manages chunks (lesson 6), and client data never passes through the master. Instead, clients locate the tablet server for a given key by traversing a three-level hierarchy of location tablets. A small file in Chubby (Google's distributed lock and coordination service, covered in lesson 11) stores the location of the root tablet; the root tablet lists the locations of several metadata tablets; and the metadata tablets list the server locations of all user tablets. Clients cache these tablet locations locally, so most reads and writes go directly to the responsible tablet server. If a tablet server crashes, the master reassigns its tablets to other servers, which reconstruct each lost memtable by replaying the dead server's commit log from GFS. Because both the commit log and the SSTables live on replicated GFS storage rather than only on the tablet server's local disk, no committed writes are lost.

Range partitioning is what makes scanning a domain in the Webtable efficient: all rows for `cnn.com` sit in a single tablet or a few adjacent tablets. For the same reason, choosing the row key is the most consequential step in designing a Bigtable schema. If your row key causes all current writes to sort next to one another, all of that traffic lands on a single tablet on a single server. Consider a fleet of sensors that each report a measurement once per second, stored in a table whose row key begins with the timestamp.

blocks.caption: Sensor readings written to four tablet servers, each holding a quarter of the row range. Pick a row-key design (time first, sensor then time, or a random prefix) and watch where the writes go; the text box says what two queries cost under each: "this sensor's last day" and "every sensor's last minute". Requests move in slow motion.
blocks.task: Find a row key that spreads the writes.

blocks.text: If the row key starts with the timestamp, every incoming measurement has a key greater than all existing keys, routing 100% of writes to the very last tablet. One tablet server receives the entire write load, fills its request queue and begins rejecting writes, while the other three servers sit idle. Splitting that overloaded tablet does not help, because all new timestamps immediately fall into the upper half of the split, creating a new hot tablet on a single server. Placing the sensor ID before the timestamp distributes writes across all tablets and keeps each sensor's history contiguous, so querying one sensor's last 24 hours requires only a short scan on one tablet; the trade-off is that querying the last minute of data across all sensors must now scan every tablet. Prepending a short hash of the sensor ID distributes writes evenly even when sensor IDs are assigned sequentially, though it scatters multi-sensor range queries across the cluster. No single row key optimises every query, so you must design the key around your highest-rate reads and writes.

This illustrates the fundamental trade-off between the two ways of partitioning a key-value store. **Range partitioning** keeps adjacent keys on the same node, making range scans fast but making the cluster vulnerable to write hot spots when keys increase monotonically. **Hash partitioning** assigns each key to a node based on a cryptographic or non-cryptographic hash, spreading writes evenly across servers but forcing any range scan to query every node in the cluster. Memcached's consistent hashing ring (lesson 5) and Amazon's Dynamo (lesson 12) partition by hash, whereas Bigtable and Spanner (lesson 20) partition by range. Because a range-partitioned table can sort rows in only one key order, supporting a second access pattern (such as querying sensor readings both by sensor ID and by building ID) usually requires maintaining a second index table keyed by the alternative prefix. When a client writes to both tables without multi-row transactions, the application must handle partial failures where one write succeeds and the other fails.

Bigtable provides atomicity only within a single row. When an operation must update two rows consistently, such as transferring funds between two accounts or updating a secondary index row alongside a primary data row, the client application must handle cases where one write succeeds and the other fails. In the 2006 paper, the authors argued that most Google applications did not need multi-row transactions. A few years later, however, Jeff Dean noted that omitting distributed transactions had been a mistake: application teams needed them often enough that many implemented their own ad-hoc transaction protocols on top of Bigtable, frequently introducing bugs. Google later built Megastore and then Spanner (lesson 20) specifically to provide multi-row transactions across range-partitioned tablets.

Bigtable's architecture, with a single master assigning tablets, Chubby coordinating metadata and GFS storing durable files, follows the same separation of concerns as GFS in lessons 6 and 7: centralise placement decisions in a lightweight master while delegating data replication and durability to a shared storage layer underneath. Google made Bigtable available to external customers as Cloud Bigtable in 2015, preserving the same data model and client API.

blocks.title: Before choosing a row key
points: List the reads the table must answer, with their rates.
Put what is read together next to each other in key order.
Check that the busiest writes don't all share one prefix, especially a time.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on Bigtable
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does a log-structured store such as Bigtable accept random writes far faster than a spinning disk can do random writes?
choices: Writes are appended to a log and held in a sorted table in memory, so disks write only in long runs
It keeps every write in memory and writes nothing to disk until the machine is shut down
It spreads each write over many disks at once, so that every disk does only a small fraction of each seek
items.why: A seek costs about 10 ms; appending costs only bandwidth. The commit log makes each write durable by appending, and the memtable is written out whole as an SSTable.

items.ask: A lookup in a log-structured store finds nothing in the memtable. Without Bloom filters, roughly how many disk reads can it take?
choices: Exactly one, because the block index says which file holds the row
Up to one for each SSTable that might hold a version of the row
None, because the SSTables' contents are cached in memory as they are written
items.why: Versions of a row can be in any SSTable, so a read checks each, newest first. Compaction keeps the count small and Bloom filters skip files that can't hold the key.

items.ask: What does a Bloom filter on an SSTable tell a read?
choices: Which 64 KB block of the file holds the key, so only one block is read
The newest timestamp in the file, so older files can be skipped
That the key is certainly not in the file, or that it probably is
items.why: A Bloom filter never says no to a key that was added, and says yes to a key that wasn't only rarely (about 1% at 10 bits per key), so most files can be skipped without a disk read.

items.ask: What does compaction cost a log-structured store?
choices: Nothing on disk, since it only removes files; it costs some memory while it runs
Extra disk writes: the same data is rewritten each time it is merged into a bigger file
Lost writes: rows changed while a compaction runs must be written again by the client
items.why: Merging reads files and writes new ones, so each byte is written several times in all. That write amplification is the price of cheap reads and of reclaiming space.

items.ask: A table stores readings from 100,000 sensors with the row key "timestamp#sensorID". Writes are slow while most tablet servers sit idle. Why?
choices: Every new row sorts after all existing rows, so all writes land in the last tablet
The timestamps make every key unique, so Bloom filters cannot skip any files
Range partitioning sends each sensor to a random tablet, so writes for one sensor collide
items.why: Tablets hold row ranges. Keys that grow with time all fall at the end of the range, onto one server, however the earlier rows were split.

items.ask: The same sensor table must answer "all readings of one sensor for a day" thousands of times a second, and "all sensors' last minute" once a minute. Which row key fits best?
choices: timestamp#sensorID, so the once-a-minute summary of every sensor is one short scan
a random number per row, to spread load
sensorID#timestamp, so one sensor's day is one short scan
items.why: The frequent query decides the key. With the sensor first, its readings are contiguous; the all-sensor query must ask every tablet, a cost paid once a minute instead of thousands of times a second.

items.ask: What is the main trade between partitioning a table by key range and by hash of the key?
choices: Ranges suit scans but invite hot spots; hashes spread load but scatter scans
Ranges need a master to assign them while hashes need none, and both scan equally well
Hashes keep neighbouring keys together for scans; ranges spread load evenly but scatter scans
items.why: Sorted ranges put similar keys on one server, good for scans and bad when the busy keys are similar. A hash puts each key somewhere unrelated to its neighbours.

rows.title: Why only one row
rows.text: Each row lives in exactly one tablet on one server, so an atomic change to it needs no coordination with any other machine. An atomic change to two rows on two servers needs a protocol that lets both agree to commit or both abort, which lesson 20 shows is slow and can block.

tombstone.title: Tombstones
tombstone.text: A delete cannot remove a value from an SSTable that is never modified, so it is written as a new entry that says "deleted". Reads that meet it ignore older versions. Only a compaction that merges every file holding the row can drop the tombstone and the data under it together; drop it earlier, and an older value in another file would come back.

bloom.title: Bloom filter arithmetic
bloom.text: With m bits per key and the best number of hash functions (m × ln 2, about 7 for 10 bits), the false-positive rate is about 0.6185 to the power m. Ten bits give 0.8%; 9.6 bits give 1%; each extra 4.8 bits divides the rate by ten.

bmdiff.title: A web page and its copies
bmdiff.text: Versions of the same page are nearly identical, and so are pages of one site, which sit next to each other in the Webtable. The paper used a compression scheme that looks for long repeated strings across a whole block, and reports the Webtable shrinking to about a tenth of its size, much better than compressing each page alone.
